en: Then, having approached the self-existent Grandfather of the worlds, seated comfortably in the Brahma-world, Kāśyapa questioned him. ||1||
What is the measure of edible things by night or by day?
Tell me, who am asking you, everything concerning that which pertains to the moon and the sun. (2)
As that high-souled Kārayapa was listening,
the Blessed One proclaimed the entire supreme knowledge of the auspicious moments (muhūrta).
Twelve *acchinimeṣas* are designated as one *lava*;
thirty *lavas* are known as one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* constitute one *liptā*. (4)
There should be thirty beads for the purpose of the muhūrta;
its length should be twelve finger-breadths according to measurement. (5)
One should illuminate that western direction with ninety-six finger-breadths;
at the time of twilight in the east, it is called the fierce (raudra) color.
The Śveta is declared to be sixty [aṅgulas], while the Maitra is twelve aṅgulas;
that which is six [aṅgulas] is the Sārabhaṭa, and the Sāvitra is recorded as being five [aṅgulas]. ||7||
The All-Prosperous One likewise fashioned that fourfold Vairāja among the [sacrificial] bricks;
at midday we shall inhale it, in which the Āyā is established. 8.
The shadow that moves toward the east occurs during three Rohiṇīs;
it is known as Bala in four [Rohiṇīs] and remembered as Vijaya in five.
The Nairṛta [altar] is six finger-breadths, the Vāruṇa twelve finger-breadths,
the Saumya is declared to be sixty, and the Bhaga is likewise supreme.
These twelve muhūrtas have been explained; they are likewise [to be known] by age.
However, others should be understood to exist during the night as well; of this there is no doubt.
Henceforth, however, listen as I explain in detail and in its entirety the auspicious and inauspicious [results] for all [beings] in their proper sequence. 12.1.
In the Raudra [mudrā], one should constantly perform fierce acts and all tasks pertaining to Rudra;
whatever may be fierce, all that should be accomplished by means of this.
In Śveta, bathing, villages, gardens, as well as agriculture, and undertakings succeed; and whatever matters are contemplated there, they are accomplished in some way. || 2 ||
One should always perform acts of friendship; one should never act otherwise. One should ensure that no enmity arises at all, and have everything accomplished through this means.
One should perform the rite of sorcery against enemies using sārabhaṭa;
whether for one's own sake or for the sake of a friend, those enemies shall perish. ||4||
Within a moment, one should perform the rites for the gods,
as well as sacrifices, marriages, and the ceremonies of tonsure and initiation.
During the Vairāja Muhūrta, one should undertake royal prowess;
one should cause the vital points, the bestowals of wealth, and the acts of an enemy to be performed.
Under Viśvāvasu, however, one should cause all undertakings to begin;
and for all the twice-born, the private recitation of the Vedas (svādhyāya) is praised.
For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and also for Śūdras— for all the social classes alike— the yoga of Abhijit occurs daily at midday.
Abhijit is for the fulfillment of all desires through the accomplishment of all purposes and tasks, for those accumulating wealth and for those wishing to travel upon the road. (9)
The trees, bimba-fruit trees, shrubs, and creepers planted in Rauhiṇa were always free from disease, abounding in flowers, and laden with fruit.
But a king, having personally mounted his own force, should employ that force against the enemy's force;
through such strategic application, he should accomplish his purpose and conquer his foes even in difficult circumstances. (11) 2.
For one who sets out with victory, there is no doubt that victory will follow;
one should perform auspicious rites, as well as propitiatory and health-promoting ceremonies. (1)
One should illuminate the army in the southwest and crush the enemy kingdom;
this [mudrā] brings prosperity to the performer and destroys all enemies without exception.
During the Vāruṇa Muhūrta,
one should sow the seeds of barley, wheat, rice, sugarcane, and blue lotuses.
In the north, one should always perform gentle acts and all lunar rites;
whatever may be gentle, one should cause all of that to be done there.
One should apply the charms for good fortune upon the vulva of all women, and especially that of maidens, O you of terrible prowess! (5)
Through fortune, O knower of the excellent Veda, one obtains a maiden who increases the Brāhmaṇa lineage;
a maiden chosen through fortune never goes elsewhere. //6//3//
On the night of the first day of the bright fortnight, on the fifth day at night, likewise on the eighth day at night, and also on the twelfth day by day, the first Karaṇa begins. || 1 ||
On the night of the full moon, [one should worship] the new [image]; on the fourth day, again by day;
on the night of the seventh day, that very same [image]; and on the eleventh day, by day. ||2||
Understand that the instruments [of action] are bound by the auspicious and the inauspicious;
having realized them in their true nature, a person shall not encounter calamity. (3)
A month is constituted by eleven karaṇas;
O Bhavānī, among them, four are moving and seven are fixed.
Nava, Pālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi is the seventh. ||5||
Śakuni, Catuṣpada, Nāga, and Kaustuma as the fourth;
I shall now describe individually the specific function of each one.
But on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at night, one should first employ the bird named Śakuni for the purpose of seizing [the enemy] as well as for flight. (7)
This is praised in all matters: for servants, for warriors, for the rearing of domestic birds, for medical treatment, and in battle.
One should offer the *bhūtatantra* oblation (*bali*) that slays enemies;
this is the ritual known as *catuṣpada*, performed on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight during the day.
It is beneficial for all quadrupeds in all their activities;
therefore, a man should perform a śrāddha here and remain self-restrained.
One should cause all these tasks involving water to be performed;
on the night of the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, the Karaṇa is said to be Nāga.
One should declare that what is lost is lost, and likewise that what is bound will end there; so too regarding those tasks that must be performed and the seizing of the enemy's forces.
On the first day of the bright fortnight, during the daytime, Kaustubha shall be the Karaṇa;
it is known as Vaiśvadeva and is praised for all undertakings. (1)
One should perform both fixed and swift rites during the Bava Karana;
for that indeed accomplishes all objectives during both departure and entry. (2)
The Bālava karana is auspicious for Brahmins in all undertakings, such as the tonsure ceremony, the initiation ceremony, sacrifices, marriages, and rites for prosperity.
The commencement of the three pure castes is prescribed, except in the case of the auspicious king, for the sake of rites for peace and prosperity. (4)
One should perform those actions associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), as well as those that bring about success (*siddhi*) and stationary tasks, during the *kaulava* karana. ||5||
One should cause the construction of the royal gate to begin on a Tuesday;
this procedure is always most excellent for those who serve the king.
Various ornaments and divine decorations, as well as other appropriate remedies for those who are afflicted, were likewise prepared.
One should perform with a hide from a black antelope whatever task belongs to householders, as well as the rearing of cattle and the practice of buying and selling. (8)
One should cause the entry into houses, the laying out of sites, the construction of dwellings, and especially tasks such as plowing and so forth, to be carried out [under these auspices]. ||9||
For a merchant among merchants, this is auspicious in all transactions;
the seller prospers therein, and the buyer does not suffer loss. (10)
One should neither perform nor cause to be performed any work during Viṣṭi and Karakha; even if a task is accomplished with great difficulty, its resulting fruit will be meager.
If that rite should ever be accomplished by a laborer,
it cannot be endured for long even by the gods.
Viṣṭi, when it arrives at its head, brings about the destruction of wealth;
in the middle, it is known to be life-taking; but in the tail, there is certain victory. (13)
One should know that five ghaṭikās belong to Bhāga, fourteen to Vartamāna, and eight to Madhya; these are remembered as the ages of Viṣṭi's tail (puccha).
Garuda is the deity of the bird, the bull of the four-footed creatures, the Nagas of the serpent, and the Lord of Wealth (Kuvera) of the Kaustubha gem. ||15||
Viṣṇu is the deity of Nava; Prajāpati is the deity of Bālava; Soma is the deity of Kaulava; and Śatakratu is the deity of Taitila. ||16||
Garāḍi has Jīva as its deity, while Maṇibhadra is the deity of Vaṇija;
Mṛtyu is proclaimed to be the deity of Viṣṭi. ||17||

"Kavi" (Mercury), "Rasa" (Venus), "Divā" (Day), "Adara" (Jupiter), "Bhūta" (Mars), "Divā-śuci" (the Sun), and "Aṣṭa-divākara-pūrṇa-divā" (the Moon)—these are the *viṣṭi* days for taking up work during the day; and work performed at night on these days shall quickly become auspicious. ||18||5||
At the outset, the hero should avoid the first lunar day when setting out on a journey; for one who has departed on the second day, it indicates the attainment of success and wealth. || 1 ||
The third is health, the fourth is fear of death;
the fifth is Vijayā, which is most excellent and indeed the accomplisher of all aims. (2)
The sixth [day] is for the sake of obtaining a son; the seventh, however, brings one a share of food. The eighth leads to the acquisition of health, but on the ninth, one does not return.
On the tenth day, the king sets out and trembles for the sake of gaining territory;
however, the eleventh day is praised in all places for all undertakings. (4)

The twelfth day (dvādaśī) leads to the destruction of wealth; the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) causes one's actions to waver; and the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) brings about various other misfortunes. ||5||
There should be no journey on the new moon day, nor likewise during the day on the full moon day;
for one who sets out on the full moon day, success does not arise.
One should avoid the sixth, eighth, ninth, fourth, and fifth lunar days; one should also avoid the fourteenth day, even if it is otherwise endowed with an auspicious constellation.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā as the fifth—these five lunar days (tithis) are to be known in both fortnights. 8.
One should know that the first lunar day (pratipad) is Nandā, as are the sixth and eleventh;
the second and seventh are Bhadrā, and the twelfth is Upapadyā. (9)
The third and the eighth are indeed Jayā, as is the thirteenth;
the fourth, the ninth, and likewise the fourteenth are Riktā. (10)
The fifth, the tenth, the full moon day, and likewise the fifteenth—these lunar days, when combined with these two weekdays, are successful for you; listen to that. (11)
One should observe Nandā on a Saturday and a Wednesday, Madrā on a Tuesday, Jayā on a Sunday, and Riktā on a Friday;
Pūrṇā is auspicious on a Thursday. These five [tithis] on these five [days] bring victory and bestow all fruits.
Those who know the lunar days say that a pair of mustard seeds [placed] at the gap [of the moon's digits] indicates the new moon; it is not the second or the tenth.
Odd-numbered days are most excellent; all undertakings on the third and ninth days should be avoided. (13.6)
In Nandā, one should enjoy various kinds of food and drink, ornaments, excellent women, joy itself, and whatever else is most dear to the mind. (1)
In the *Bhadrā* [nakṣatra], one should perform auspicious aspirations, various yogic postures (*yogāsana*),
and the rites of reciting benedictions (*svastivācana*), as well as the commencement of undertakings.
On the day of Jayā, one should mobilize the army; merchants and artisans should engage in trade and sell their wares, and one should cause the work of weapons to be performed.
O Bhavānī, one who is skilled in the lunar days should always avoid all undertakings, whether stationary or moving, on the day of Rikvā.
During the month of Pūrṇā, one should cause storehouses and treasuries to be built at Setubandha;
and during the month of Pauṣa, one should cause vehicles, chariots, and carriages to be prepared.
In this very way, one should avoid performing [the rite] three times;
thus it shall yield fruit for the rites prescribed by the science of astrology.

Experts in these matters do not prescribe the performance of a journey when there is a lapse of seasons, when the moon has waned, when the fortnight has ended, when the luminaries are eclipsed, or when the groups of constellations are censured. ||7||
Regarding the period of purification that has been prescribed, for how long should it be ordained?
It should be understood that once the eleventh day has passed, one is fit to travel on the road.
Venus shall cause an accumulation of wealth, Jupiter causes delusion of the intellect, and Mars brings about a great disease; of this there is no doubt. (9)
Budha causes distress from kinsmen and exile; Śanaiścara brings about the destruction of one's position among relatives; Sūrya likewise brings fear, as does Soma.

The lunar mansion (nakṣatra) provides self-protection, while the lunar day (tithi) accomplishes one's purpose; through the karana one achieves the completion of the task, and from the muhurta one should predict gain. ||11||

A wise person should always cause the ritual to be performed by four [assistants] for the sake of attaining success, according to the lunar day, the asterism, the karana, and the auspicious moment. 12.
Furthermore, due to the distance [of the lunar day], one should always commence the ritual action by means of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), the karaṇa, and the muhūrta. (13)
Indeed, because of the great distance of the constellations, a wise person, acting with haste, should undertake his work based on two factors: the *karana* and the *muhūrta*. (14)
Indeed, because of the distance of the instrument, one should have it performed in just a moment;
an action performed in a moment succeeds—of this there is no doubt. ||15||
If the rite for one situated at a distance is performed with haste, it shall become a source of all prosperity through the chanting of "Puṇyāha" by the twice-born. ||16||
Śakuna is the leader of the fourfold knowledge consisting of the nāḍī, the muhūrta, the tithi, and the karaṇa. ||17||
The omen, the wind, the mind, and likewise one's attendants—if these are favorable, there is success indeed; of this there is no doubt. (18)
Where a woman is exceedingly weak, there the star Tārā has no power;
for a woman established in her marriage is never entitled to independence.
One should not grant [the bride] after considering the power of the moon in the dark fortnight or the strength of the stars;
for when the husband is away in a foreign land or incapacitated, the wife performs all the duties.
The merit of the lunar day (tithi) is said to be single-fold; that of the asterism (nakṣatra), fourfold;
that of the day of the week (vāra), eightfold; and that of the Karaṇa is endowed with sixteenfold [merit]. (21)
The yoga of thirty-two [degrees] is endowed with sixty stars;
it is said that the moon is multiplied by one hundred, and therefore the strength or weakness of the moon is determined.
Having considered the strengths and weaknesses of the moon, the planets bestow good and evil results;
just as the senses joined with the mind perform their functions and do not act alone, so too do these [planets]. || 23.7 ||
Āditya, Soma, Bhauma, as well as Budha, Bṛhaspati, Bhārgava, and Śanaiścara—these are the lords of the seven days. || 1 ||
The consecration of a king, the departure of a king, the king’s business, and the audience with a king—whatever task is said to be appropriate on earth, all of that is auspicious on a Sunday. (2)

One who knows the ritual rules should drink juices and the drinking of honey and soma, perform rites for good fortune, apply ointments, sow seeds in the field, and perform the *vrata* on the day of Soma. //3//

In a city or a town, the destruction of enemies, as well as the office of commander-in-chief in the kingdom, the practice of physical exercise and weaponry, and even theft of land—these are indeed always praised for a son. (4)

The arrival of an envoy for the purpose of war, for the sake of a daughter or offspring, for the business of peace with an enemy, or for the restoration of a broken counsel—these they highly praise when undertaken on a Wednesday during the day. (5)

On the day of Jupiter, one should perform Vedic study, worship of the gods, the construction of temples, purificatory rites, and the initiation of ascetics; likewise, on the day of Venus, one may engage in agriculture, as well as acquire clothing, a wife, wealth, and ornaments.
Riding on horseback for the first time, mounting an elephant,
the giving away of a daughter in marriage, and their buying and selling— these are always auspicious on a Friday.

The installation of a sacrificial post for ritual sacrifices, entering a house, the tethering of an elephant, residing in a village, a town, or a city—all these are auspicious during the period of Saturn. 8.8.

I shall proclaim the doctrine of Bhūgomin, which concerns the self, karma, and the most excellent qualities, pertaining to each individual person, concise in its composition yet of great significance.

The auspicious and inauspicious nature of the constellations, which must be discerned individually by a person, should be understood as that which brings about one's own prosperity for those who desire their own success. (2)
In the birth and activity of the nine triads, [the results] correspond respectively to the lower and higher groups. (3)

Likewise, the practitioner who is swift against the adversaries of the prosperity of birth, as well as the group of friends and the supreme friend, are the ones who bring about the end of suffering. 4.
The natal asterism (janmanakṣatra) is called the karma-nakṣatra;
the nineteenth from it is said to be the asterism for conception (garbhādhāna). ||5||
The second, eleventh, and twentieth constitute the group that brings prosperity;
however, the third, twenty-first, and twelfth bring misfortune.
One should know that the twenty-fourth is the fourth *ceṃya*, the twenty-second is the thirteenth,
the twenty-third is the fifth *pratvara*, and the twenty-fourth is the fourteenth.
The twenty-fourth is the *sādhaka*; the sixth is the fifteenth;
the twenty-fifth is the *nairdhana*; and likewise, the sixteenth is the seventh.
One should know the seventeenth as Maitra, and the twenty-sixth as the eighth;
the twenty-seventh is the supreme Maitra, and that which is the eighteenth is the ninth.
In the group of nine constellations, one should avoid the first and the third;
likewise, one should avoid the fifth and the seventh, and perform all activities with the remaining ones. || 10 ||
